title: Rotate an array by K positions (reverse whole → reverse first K → reverse rest).
shortTitle: Rotate an Array by K Positions

s1_definition.profdef: Rotating an array to the right by K positions moves each element K places to the right, with the elements that fall off the end wrapping to the front. The elegant in-place technique is the triple reversal: first reverse the entire array, then reverse the first K elements, then reverse the remaining elements. This runs in linear time with constant extra space, after first reducing K modulo the length so that rotations larger than the array are handled correctly.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India keeps a rolling window of the last few days of Rajesh's balances, and at day-end it must shift the window so the newest days appear first, wrapping the oldest around. Imagine the days written on a strip of paper. The clerk flips the whole strip over, which reverses everything, then flips just the first part back, then flips the rest back. After these three flips the strip shows the days rotated into the new arrangement, all done on the one strip without copying to a new one.
s1_definition.oneliner: Reduce K by the length, then reverse the whole array, reverse the first K, and reverse the rest.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Rotating an array to the right by K positions moves each element K places to the right, with the elements that fall off the end wrapping to the front. The elegant in-place technique is the triple reversal: first reverse the entire array, then reverse the first K elements, then reverse the remaining elements. This runs in linear time with constant extra space, after first reducing K modulo the length so that rotations larger than the array are handled correctly.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India keeps a rolling window of the last few days of Rajesh's balances, and at day-end it must shift the window so the newest days appear first, wrapping the oldest around. Imagine the days written on a strip of paper. The clerk flips the whole strip over, which reverses everything, then flips just the first part back, then flips the rest back. After these three flips the strip shows the days rotated into the new arrangement, all done on the one strip without copying to a new one.

**One line to remember:** Reduce K by the length, then reverse the whole array, reverse the first K, and reverse the rest.

sections.s2_technical:
The first essential step is to reduce K modulo the array length. If the array has length n and K is larger than n, rotating by K is the same as rotating by K modulo n, because every full n rotations return to the start. If you skip this, indices go out of range. You also handle a negative K if left rotation is allowed by converting it to the equivalent right rotation, and you treat an empty or single-element array as needing no rotation.

The triple-reversal works because reversing the whole array puts the last K elements at the front but in reverse order, and puts the first n minus K elements at the back also in reverse order. Reversing the first K elements fixes the order of the block that should lead, and reversing the remaining elements fixes the order of the trailing block. The net effect is a correct right rotation by K.

Walk through a small example to make it concrete. Take one, two, three, four, five and rotate right by two. Reverse the whole array to get five, four, three, two, one. Reverse the first two to get four, five, three, two, one. Reverse the rest to get four, five, one, two, three, which is the original rotated right by two. Each reversal is the two-pointer swap from the ends.

A senior point is comparing approaches. A naive approach copies elements into a new array at shifted positions, which is simple but uses linear extra space. Another approach rotates one step at a time K times, which is quadratic and far too slow for large K. The triple reversal is linear time and constant space, which is why it is the preferred in-place solution. There is also a juggling or cyclic-replacement algorithm that achieves the same bounds; I usually prefer triple reversal because it is the easiest to get right and to explain.

Another senior point is direction clarity. Right rotation and left rotation differ only by how you split K, and mixing them up is a common bug. I always state explicitly which direction the method rotates and document it, and I test both a small K and a K larger than the length to prove the modulo reduction works.

A small finance-domain example: `k = k % n; reverse(a, 0, n - 1); reverse(a, 0, k - 1); reverse(a, k, n - 1);` right-rotates the balance window by k in place.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India maintains a fixed-size rolling window of Rajesh's recent daily closing balances for a trend chart. At day-end the window must be rotated so the display aligns with a new reference day, effectively shifting elements by a chosen offset with wrap-around. Doing this in place avoids allocating a new window array every day for every customer, which matters at scale. Rotating the array by K with the triple reversal is exactly this.

This is exactly how array rotation works in Java — reduce K, then three reversals rearrange the window in place.

Problem 2 — The chosen offset can sometimes exceed the window length, for example when a configuration mistake sets a large shift, so the code must reduce K modulo the length to stay correct and in range rather than throwing an index error. This shows the importance of the modulo step and of handling the trivial empty and single-element cases.

What the code will do: a `WindowRotator` with `rotateRight(BigDecimal[] window, int k)` that reduces K, then performs three in-place reversals via a private reverse helper. The demo rotates Rajesh's balance window by a normal K and by a K larger than the length.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: the balance window is `100, 200, 300, 400, 500` and we rotate right by `2`.

Step 1: n is five. We normalise k as two modulo five, which stays two. It is not zero, so we rotate.

Step 2: We reverse the whole window from index zero to four, turning `100, 200, 300, 400, 500` into `500, 400, 300, 200, 100`. The last two elements are now at the front but in reversed order.

Step 3: We reverse the first k, which is indices zero to one, turning `500, 400` into `400, 500`. The window is now `400, 500, 300, 200, 100`. The leading block is now in correct order.

Step 4: We reverse the rest, indices two to four, turning `300, 200, 100` into `100, 200, 300`. The window becomes `400, 500, 100, 200, 300`, which is the original rotated right by two.

Step 5: The demo then rotates by seven. We normalise seven modulo five to two, so this is the same as another right rotation by two. Without the modulo step, k of seven would run reversals with out-of-range indices.

Step 6: The three reversals run again on the already-rotated window, producing `200, 300, 400, 500, 100`. Everything happened in place on the single window array, using only a temporary inside the reverse helper.

Final output:

```
2026-10-26T16:40:00Z INFO Before: [100, 200, 300, 400, 500]
2026-10-26T16:40:00Z INFO Rotated right by 2: [400, 500, 100, 200, 300]
2026-10-26T16:40:00Z INFO After rotateRight(2): [400, 500, 100, 200, 300]
2026-10-26T16:40:00Z INFO Rotated right by 2: [200, 300, 400, 500, 100]
2026-10-26T16:40:00Z INFO After rotateRight(7): [200, 300, 400, 500, 100]
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Input: [100,200,300,400,500], k=2
    │
    ▼
  normalise k = 2 % 5 = 2
    │ reverse all      → [500,400,300,200,100]
    │ reverse first 2  → [400,500,300,200,100]
    │ reverse rest     → [400,500,100,200,300]
    ▼
  rotated right by 2
    │
    ├─ k=7 → 7 % 5 = 2 → same triple reversal again
    ▼
  Output: [200,300,400,500,100] (oversized k handled by modulo)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Rotating an array right by K moves each element K places to the right with wrap-around, and the elegant in-place way is the triple reversal: reverse the whole array, then reverse the first K elements, then reverse the rest. It runs in linear time and constant space.

The first thing I always do is reduce K modulo the length, because rotating by more than the length is the same as rotating by K modulo the length, and skipping that step sends indices out of range. I also normalise a negative K into the equivalent right rotation and treat empty or single-element arrays as no-ops.

I can explain why the triple reversal works: reversing the whole array brings the last K elements to the front but in reverse, so reversing the first K fixes their order and reversing the remaining elements fixes the trailing block. Compared with the alternatives, copying into a new array uses linear extra space and rotating one step at a time K times is quadratic, so the triple reversal is the best in-place choice, and it is easier to get right than the cyclic juggling algorithm.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this to rotate Rajesh's rolling window of recent daily closing balances at day-end so the trend chart aligns with a new reference day, doing it in place so we do not allocate a fresh window array per customer per day. A misconfigured offset can exceed the window length, so the modulo normalisation keeps it correct and in range. Explaining the modulo step, why the three reversals produce the rotation, and the comparison with the slower alternatives shows the interviewer that I know the efficient in-place solution and its edge cases.
